articles.summary: Employee Management End-of-Year HR Checklist: How to Prepare Your Business for 2027 Oluwakemi Adesina November 27, 2026 December is one of the busiest month in most Nigerian businesses. Payroll, bonuses, the end-of-year push, then the break. An end-of-year HR review is a few days of sorting out your records, contracts and policies before the new year starts. Do it in December and January is calmer for the business. You will not finish everything, so start with what costs you money when it is wrong: employee records and compliance. A late appraisal annoys someone. A missing contract or an unpaid pension remittance can cost you a lot more. Also: · Employee details never updated after a promotion, a name change or a move. · Contracts agreed verbally and never signed, or signed and never filed. · Appraisals half-done in June and quietly abandoned. · Leave balances nobody reconciled, so nobody knows what the company owes. · Grievances “handled” in a corridor and never documented. None of these looks serious on its own. Together they are why January turns into catching up on your own records. What an end-of-year HR audit is An HR audit is a structured review of your policies, processes, records and practices. The point is to find where your records and your reality are not aligned and fix them. HR compliance audit Whether your practices and documentation line up with the obligations that apply to you, which depend on workforce size, locations and what your people do. Run it against current official guidance, not last year’s notes. Employee records audit Whether your files are accurate and complete: job titles that match what people do, start dates that match contracts, contracts filed where you can find them. It sounds like filing, but it is the foundation of next year’s decisions. HR process review How the day-to-day work runs: recruitment, onboarding, leave, performance, offboarding. If onboarding ends with a signed contract in an email draft, no audit of the files will fix that. End-of-year HR checklist for Nigerian businesses Here is the review we would actually run, roughly in order. 1. Review and update employee records Pull every active file and check it against reality: contact and emergency details, job titles, start dates, reporting lines, contract, salary and benefits. We have lost count of how often a “Head of Sales” is still recorded as a sales executive. Our guide to employee records management in Nigeria covers what a complete file should hold. 2. Review employment contracts and documentation Check that everyone has a documented contract, that job descriptions match what people do now, that promotions were recorded rather than agreed in a meeting, and that fixed-term agreements are reviewed before they lapse. The common failure is the informal promotion: a bigger role and a new salary, but a contract nobody updated, so two years later both sides rely on different versions of the truth. 3. Review and update HR policies Check the policies your team actually lives by: attendance, leave, remote and hybrid working, code of conduct, disciplinary and grievance procedures, data protection, health and safety, and benefits. A remote work policy written for a fully in-office team, still applied two years into hybrid work, is a set of rules nobody follows and a standard nobody can enforce. 4. Complete employee performance reviews Close out the year’s appraisals: review objectives against what was achieved, document outcomes, capture feedback, and agree 2027 objectives. A review is only defensible if it rests on expectations set earlier and documented outcomes, not a manager’s memory in December. 5. Review employee leave and attendance records Reconcile leave taken and outstanding, sick leave, unapproved absences and the year’s attendance record, and confirm your public holiday arrangements. When approvals live in WhatsApp and memory, nobody can say what is owed, so someone is short-changed and nobody notices. 6. Review employee training and development Look at what training actually happened against what was planned, where the skills gaps are, and which capabilities the business will need in 2027, then build next year’s calendar from that. Reviewing training against the business plan is what turns a budget into capability. 7. Review employee benefits and welfare Check health insurance, pension-related employee information, allowances and welfare initiatives, whether all of it was documented and communicated, and whether it is still relevant and affordable. Benefits drift in two directions: promised informally and never documented, or inherited from another era and kept out of habit. Our guide to employee benefits in Nigeria sets out what is mandatory and what is a choice. 8. Review recruitment and employee turnover Pull the numbers: how many you hired and lost, what recruitment cost, how long vacancies took to fill, and why people left where you know. Identify the critical roles that would hurt if the person walked. This is the section most businesses skip because it feels like reporting; it is the most useful one for next year’s budget. 9. Review employee grievances and workplace issues Go through unresolved complaints, disciplinary cases and workplace conflicts, and confirm issues were documented, handled confidentially, and resolved through a fair process. An unresolved grievance does not disappear, it waits, and your best protection in any dispute is a documented, fair process that was actually followed. 10. Review HR compliance requirements Map the obligations that actually apply to you and check your records against them: employment documentation, labour requirements, health and safety, pension responsibilities, data protection, and the tax and statutory records you must keep. Run this against current guidance, not last year’s understanding. articles.summary: Galvanic facility utilizes automation to reduce production lead times of key components for civil, commercial and military aircraft engines KALISZ, Poland (Nov. 27, 2026) — Pratt & Whitney, an RTX (NYSE: RTX) business, today announced the opening of a new galvanic facility at its Kalisz site, which manufactures precision components for multiple aircraft engine types serving civil, commercial and military operators around the world. By bringing galvanic processing capability in-house, Pratt & Whitney is strengthening control over its manufacturing process, improving quality, reducing production lead times and providing additional capacity to meet industry demand. Galvanic facilities perform a key function in aerospace manufacturing, enabling the metallic plating of components for durability and corrosion resistance. The new facility combines an automated galvanizing process with high standards of environmental and safety controls. It reduces the use of hazardous chemicals and manages water usage with a closed-loop system that enables full neutralization of water and removal of waste material. The facility also features advanced safety systems, including gas detection systems, redundant safety sensors and safety gates that automatically stop production lines. “The new galvanic facility marks another step in the development of Kalisz as a hub for advanced aerospace manufacturing and confirms Poland’s strategic importance to RTX,” said Wojciech Wasik, executive director, Board President, Pratt & Whitney Kalisz. “We are investing in technology, infrastructure and our employees’ skills, combining the highest standards of quality, safety and management of waste material.” Operating since 1992, the Kalisz site is an important part of Pratt & Whitney’s global manufacturing network, producing components for multiple engine types, ranging from turboprops to military engines. Kalisz is also a center of excellence for geared components, including the fan drive gear system featured on the Pratt & Whitney GTF™ engines that power the latest generation of single-aisle aircraft such as the Airbus A220, A320neo and Embraer E2 families. The project represents an investment of $12.5 million, which was supported by the Generator of Ecological Concepts, a joint program of Poland’s National Centre for Research and Development and the National Fund for Environmental Protection and Water Management. Poland represents RTX's largest investment and employee base outside the United States, with more than 9,500 employees across its Collins Aerospace, Pratt & Whitney and Raytheon businesses in-country. More than 1,700 employees are based in Kalisz. About Pratt & Whitney Pratt & Whitney, an RTX business, is a world leader in the design, manufacture and service of aircraft engines and auxiliary power units for military, commercial and civil aviation customers. Since 1925, our engineers have pioneered the development of revolutionary aircraft propulsion technologies, and today we support more than 90,000 in-service engines through our global network of maintenance, repair and overhaul facilities. About RTX With more than 180,000 global employees, we push the limits of technology and science to redefine how we connect and protect our world. With industry-leading capabilities, we advance aviation, engineer integrated defence systems for operational success, and develop next-generation technology solutions and manufacturing to help global customers address their most critical challenges. The company, with 2025 sales of more than $88 billion, is headquartered in Arlington, Virginia. For questions or to schedule an interview, please contact corporatepr@rtx.com. SOURCE RTX
